notes.front: What is cloud computing?
notes.back: The on-demand delivery of compute power, databases, storage, applications and other resources over the internet, with pay-as-you-go pricing.
notes.explanation: It replaces large upfront investments in hardware, and the heavy lifting of managing that hardware, with resources you provision as you need them.
notes.example: Like renting a van by the hour instead of buying a fleet, but for servers and storage you reach over the internet.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “What is cloud computing?”
notes.evidence: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute power, database, storage, applications, and other IT resources through a cloud services platform via the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.

notes.front: In the six advantages of cloud computing, what is a variable expense?
notes.back: Spending that follows use: you pay only when you consume computing resources, and only for how much you consume.
notes.explanation: It is the alternative to investing heavily in data centres and servers before you know how you will use them.
notes.example: Like a metered electricity bill instead of building your own power station, but for computing.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: Instead of having to invest heavily in data centers and servers before you know how you’re going to use them, you can pay only when you consume computing resources, and pay only for how much you consume.

notes.front: What are economies of scale, as an advantage of cloud computing?
notes.back: Lower pay-as-you-go prices that a provider can offer because it aggregates the usage of hundreds of thousands of customers.
notes.explanation: The whitepaper says this gives you a lower variable cost than you could get on your own.
notes.example: Like a supermarket chain that buys in bulk and charges less per tin than a corner shop can.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: By using cloud computing, you can achieve a lower variable cost than you can get on your own. Because usage from hundreds of thousands of customers is aggregated in the cloud, providers such as AWS can achieve higher economies of scale, which translates into lower pay as-you-go prices.

notes.front: What does the advantage "stop guessing capacity" mean?
notes.back: You no longer have to decide your infrastructure capacity before you deploy: you use as much or as little as you need.
notes.explanation: The whitepaper calls it eliminating guesswork about your infrastructure capacity needs.
notes.example: Like a theatre that could add or remove seats for each night’s audience, instead of building for the biggest crowd it might ever get.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: Eliminate guessing on your infrastructure capacity needs. When you make a capacity decision prior to deploying an application, you often end up either sitting on expensive idle resources or dealing with limited capacity.

notes.front: What does agility mean in the advantage "increase speed and agility"?
notes.back: An organisation’s ability to experiment and develop quickly, because new resources are only a click away.
notes.explanation: The whitepaper links the increase in agility to the much lower cost and time it takes to experiment and develop.
notes.example: Like a kitchen where a chef can try a new dish tonight because the ingredients are already on the shelf, instead of ordering them for next month.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: In a cloud computing environment, new IT resources are only a click away, which means that you reduce the time to make those resources available to your developers from weeks to just minutes. This results in a dramatic increase in agility for the organization, since the cost and time it takes to experiment and develop is significantly lower.

notes.front: What is elasticity in the cloud?
notes.back: Capacity that adjusts automatically to what an application needs, which auto scaling provides by monitoring applications and adjusting capacity.
notes.explanation: Auto scaling adjusts capacity to keep performance steady and predictable at the lowest possible cost.
notes.example: Like a taxi firm that calls in extra drivers when a concert ends and sends them home afterwards, but done automatically for servers.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Management and governance: AWS Auto Scaling”
notes.evidence: AWS Auto Scaling monitors your applications and automatically adjusts capacity to maintain steady, predictable performance at the lowest possible cost.

notes.front: What is high availability?
notes.back: Keeping an application available when a failure hits one location, instead of hosting everything in a single location.
notes.explanation: Failures are rare, but if every instance sits in one location that fails, none of the instances is available.
notes.example: Like a bank with branches in two towns, so customers can still be served if one branch floods.
notes.source: Amazon EC2 User Guide, “Regions and Zones”
notes.evidence: Although rare, failures can occur that affect the availability of instances that are in the same location. If you host all of your instances in a single location that is affected by a failure, none of your instances would be available.

notes.front: What is the Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model?
notes.back: Re-purposing your existing software licence inventory for use with your cloud resources.
notes.explanation: The License Manager guide presents it as a way to save costs as you build out your cloud infrastructure.
notes.example: Like taking your own season ticket to a partner venue instead of buying a new one, but for database software licences.
notes.source: AWS License Manager User Guide, “What is AWS License Manager?”
notes.evidence: As you build out your cloud infrastructure on AWS, you can save costs by using Bring Your Own License model (BYOL) opportunities. That is, you can re-purpose your existing license inventory for use with your cloud resources.

notes.front: What is rightsizing?
notes.back: Downsizing instances that are idle or have low utilisation, so that you stop paying for capacity you do not use.
notes.explanation: The pricing whitepaper gives it as a way to reduce costs once a report has shown which instances are idle or under-used.
notes.example: Like moving a four-person team out of a twenty-desk office into a six-desk one, but for a virtual server.
notes.source: How AWS Pricing Works (historical reference), “AWS Cost Optimization: Match capacity with demand”
notes.evidence: Use AWS Cost Explorer Resource Optimization to get a report of Amazon EC2 instances that are either idle or have low utilization. You can reduce costs by either stopping or downsizing these instances.

notes.front: What is automation, as a benefit of the cloud?
notes.back: Creating and replicating workloads through automated processes rather than manual effort, at low cost.
notes.explanation: The Well-Architected Framework says it avoids the expense of manual effort.
notes.example: Like a bread machine that bakes the same loaf every time from one recipe, but for building servers and networks.
notes.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, “General design principles”
notes.evidence: Automation permits you to create and replicate your workloads at low cost and avoid the expense of manual effort.

notes.front: In cloud computing, who owns and maintains the network-connected hardware?
notes.back: The cloud services platform, such as Amazon Web Services; you provision and use what you need through a web application.
notes.explanation: You get servers, storage, databases and application services over the internet without owning the machines behind them.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “What is cloud computing?”
notes.evidence: Cloud computing provides a simple way to access servers, storage, databases and a broad set of application services over the internet. A cloud services platform such as Amazon Web Services owns and maintains the network-connected hardware required for these application services, while you provision and use what you need via a web application.

notes.front: Which fixed expenses does the pricing whitepaper say the cloud lets you trade for variable expenses?
notes.back: Data centres and physical servers.
notes.explanation: After the trade you pay for information technology only as you consume it.
notes.source: How AWS Pricing Works (historical reference), “Key principles: Start early with cost optimization”
notes.evidence: The cloud allows you to trade fixed expenses (such as data centers and physical servers) for variable expenses, and only pay for IT as you consume it.

notes.front: What two problems does a capacity decision made before deploying an application often cause?
notes.back: Sitting on expensive idle resources, or dealing with limited capacity.
notes.explanation: A guess made up front is usually either too high or too low; the whitepaper says cloud computing makes these problems go away.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: When you make a capacity decision prior to deploying an application, you often end up either sitting on expensive idle resources or dealing with limited capacity. With cloud computing, these problems go away.

notes.front: According to the six advantages, how far can the cloud cut the time to make new resources available to developers?
notes.back: From weeks to just minutes.
notes.explanation: New resources are only a click away, and the whitepaper ties the resulting drop in cost and time to experiment to greater agility.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: new IT resources are only a click away, which means that you reduce the time to make those resources available to your developers from weeks to just minutes.

notes.front: Which advantage of cloud computing lets you focus on your own customers rather than on racking, stacking and powering servers?
notes.back: Stop spending money running and maintaining data centres.
notes.explanation: The whitepaper frames it as putting effort into projects that differentiate your business, not into infrastructure.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers – Focus on projects that differentiate your business, not the infrastructure. Cloud computing lets you focus on your own customers, rather than on the heavy lifting of racking, stacking, and powering servers.

notes.front: Which advantage of cloud computing is about deploying an application in multiple Regions around the world with a few clicks?
notes.back: Go global in minutes.
notes.explanation: Deploying in many Regions lets you give customers lower latency and a better experience at minimal cost.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: Go global in minutes – Easily deploy your application in multiple regions around the world with just a few clicks. This means you can provide lower latency and a better experience for your customers at minimal cost.

notes.front: The exam guide expects you to recognise that {{c1::auto scaling}} provides elasticity.
notes.explanation: Auto scaling is the mechanism the guide names; elasticity is the property it gives a workload.
notes.source: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) Exam Guide, “Content Domain 3: Cloud Technology and Services, Task Statement 3.3”
notes.evidence: Recognizing that auto scaling provides elasticity

notes.front: How can you protect your applications from the failure of a single location in a Region?
notes.back: Launch instances in multiple Availability Zones.
notes.explanation: Spreading instances across zones means that one location’s failure need not take every instance down.
notes.source: Amazon EC2 User Guide, “Regions and Zones”
notes.evidence: By launching EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones, you can protect your applications from the failure of a single location in the Region.

notes.front: Your instances are spread across several Availability Zones and one instance fails. What can a well-designed application do?
notes.back: Have an instance in another Availability Zone handle the requests instead.
notes.explanation: The guide says you can design your application this way; spreading instances alone does not reroute the requests.
notes.source: Amazon EC2 User Guide, “Regions and Zones”
notes.evidence: If you distribute instances across multiple Availability Zones and an instance fails, you can design your application so that an instance in another Availability Zone handles requests instead.

notes.front: Besides Bring Your Own License (BYOL) opportunities, what does License Manager give an organisation?
notes.back: Consolidated visibility and reporting for software licence compliance, which limits licensing overages and the risk of non-compliance.
notes.explanation: Tracking licences centrally matters when you re-use them across many Regions and accounts, where overages are easy to miss.
notes.source: AWS License Manager User Guide, “What is AWS License Manager?”
notes.evidence: offering consolidated visibility and comprehensive reporting for software license compliance at scale. This enables you to limit licensing overages and reduce the risk of non-compliance and misreporting.

notes.front: In the pricing whitepaper, which report shows the instances that are idle or have low utilisation?
notes.back: Cost Explorer Resource Optimization.
notes.explanation: The report tells you which instances to stop or downsize; the whitepaper is historical, so the feature’s current name may differ.
notes.source: How AWS Pricing Works (historical reference), “AWS Cost Optimization: Match capacity with demand”
notes.evidence: Use AWS Cost Explorer Resource Optimization to get a report of Amazon EC2 instances that are either idle or have low utilization.

notes.front: For idle or low-utilisation instances, you can reduce costs by either {{c1::stopping}} or downsizing them.
notes.explanation: Downsizing is rightsizing; stopping suits instances that need not run at all, and a scheduler can stop them automatically.
notes.source: How AWS Pricing Works (historical reference), “AWS Cost Optimization: Match capacity with demand”
notes.evidence: You can reduce costs by either stopping or downsizing these instances. Use AWS Instance Scheduler to automatically stop instances.

notes.front: With automation you can track changes, audit their impact and {{c1::revert to previous parameters}} when necessary.
notes.explanation: The principle pairs making changes cheaply with being able to see, check and undo them afterwards.
notes.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, “General design principles”
notes.evidence: You can track changes to your automation, audit the impact, and revert to previous parameters when necessary.

notes.front: In the cloud, what does the capability to automate and test on demand lower?
notes.back: The risk of impact from design changes.
notes.explanation: Lower risk lets systems evolve over time, so businesses can take advantage of innovations as a standard practice.
notes.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, “General design principles”
notes.evidence: In the cloud, the capability to automate and test on demand lowers the risk of impact from design changes. This permits systems to evolve over time so that businesses can take advantage of innovations as a standard practice.

notes.front: What are the three fundamental drivers of cost with Amazon Web Services?
notes.back: Compute, storage and outbound data transfer.
notes.explanation: How much each matters varies somewhat with the product and the pricing model you choose.
notes.source: How AWS Pricing Works (historical reference), “Key principles: Understand the fundamentals of pricing”
notes.evidence: There are three fundamental drivers of cost with AWS: compute, storage, and outbound data transfer. These characteristics vary somewhat, depending on the AWS product and pricing model you choose.

notes.front: How are compute resources charged, according to the pricing fundamentals?
notes.back: By the hour or by the second, from launch until you stop or terminate the resource, unless a reservation agreed the cost beforehand.
notes.explanation: Billing runs only while the resource exists and runs, which is what makes compute a variable expense.
notes.source: How AWS Pricing Works (historical reference), “Key principles: Understand the fundamentals of pricing”
notes.evidence: For compute resources, you pay by the hour or by the second from the time you launch a resource until the time you stop or terminate it, unless you have made a reservation for which the cost is agreed upon beforehand.

notes.front: Which cost driver appears on the monthly statement as Data Transfer Out?
notes.back: Outbound data transfer.
notes.explanation: It is aggregated across services and then charged at a single outbound data transfer rate, rather than service by service.
notes.source: How AWS Pricing Works (historical reference), “Key principles: Understand the fundamentals of pricing”
notes.evidence: Outbound data transfer is aggregated across services and then charged at the outbound data transfer rate. This charge appears on the monthly statement as AWS Data Transfer Out

notes.front: In most cases, there is {{c1::no charge}} for inbound data transfer or for data transfer between services within the same Region.
notes.explanation: The whitepaper hedges this: there are some exceptions, so verify data transfer rates before you begin.
notes.source: How AWS Pricing Works (historical reference), “Key principles: Understand the fundamentals of pricing”
notes.evidence: In most cases, there is no charge for inbound data transfer or for data transfer between other AWS services within the same Region. There are some exceptions, so be sure to verify data transfer rates before beginning.

notes.front: Compared with security in your on-premises data centres, which costs does security in the cloud avoid?
notes.back: The costs of maintaining facilities and hardware.
notes.explanation: In the cloud you do not manage physical servers or storage devices; you use software-based tools instead.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Security and compliance: Security”
notes.evidence: Security in the cloud is much like security in your on-premises data centers—only without the costs of maintaining facilities and hardware. In the cloud, you don’t have to manage physical servers or storage devices.

notes.front: In a traditional, on-premises solution, what are two tasks you must do yourself before a system runs?
notes.back: Any two of: capacity analysis, procuring hardware and software, installing and administering systems, testing and debugging the installation.
notes.explanation: These are the on-premises costs in effort that a managed cloud service takes over.
notes.source: AWS Database Migration Service User Guide, “Migration tasks that AWS DMS performs”
notes.evidence: In a traditional solution, you need to perform capacity analysis, procure hardware and software, install and administer systems, and test and debug the installation.

notes.front: A garden-furniture seller gets most of its web traffic in six spring weeks. It does not want to buy servers sized for spring that sit idle all year. Which advantage of cloud computing answers this?
notes.back: B: Stop guessing capacity
notes.choices:
A) Go global in minutes
B) Stop guessing capacity
C) Benefit from massive economies of scale
D) Stop spending money running and maintaining data centres
notes.choicesExplained: A is about reaching customers in many Regions, not about sizing. C is about the provider’s lower prices from aggregated usage. D is about not racking and powering servers yourself; it does not remove the sizing guess.
notes.explanation: Deciding capacity up front leaves you with idle resources or too little capacity; in the cloud you use as much or as little as you need.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: When you make a capacity decision prior to deploying an application, you often end up either sitting on expensive idle resources or dealing with limited capacity. With cloud computing, these problems go away.

notes.front: A language-learning app based in one country gains many users on two other continents, who complain of slow responses. The firm has no staff abroad. Which advantage of cloud computing helps most?
notes.back: D: Go global in minutes
notes.choices:
A) Trade fixed expense for variable expense
B) Increase speed and agility
C) Benefit from massive economies of scale
D) Go global in minutes
notes.choicesExplained: A is about how you pay, not where the application runs. B is about how fast developers get resources. C is about lower prices from aggregated usage; none of them moves the application nearer the users.
notes.explanation: Deploying in Regions near those users is a few clicks, and gives them lower latency at minimal cost.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: Easily deploy your application in multiple regions around the world with just a few clicks. This means you can provide lower latency and a better experience for your customers at minimal cost.

notes.front: A finance director would rather not approve a large server purchase before a new product has any customers. She wants the bill to track actual use. Which advantage fits?
notes.back: A: Trade fixed expense for variable expense
notes.choices:
A) Trade fixed expense for variable expense
B) Stop guessing capacity
C) Go global in minutes
D) Increase speed and agility
notes.choicesExplained: B is about sizing capacity rather than how it is paid for. C is about deploying in many Regions. D is about how quickly developers get resources.
notes.explanation: Paying only when, and as much as, you consume replaces investing heavily before you know how the servers will be used.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: Instead of having to invest heavily in data centers and servers before you know how you’re going to use them, you can pay only when you consume computing resources, and pay only for how much you consume.

notes.front: Developers at an insurer wait about a month for each test server, so they rarely try new ideas. After moving to the cloud they get servers in minutes and experiment weekly. Which advantage have they gained?
notes.back: C: Increase speed and agility
notes.choices:
A) Benefit from massive economies of scale
B) Go global in minutes
C) Increase speed and agility
D) Stop guessing capacity
notes.choicesExplained: A is about lower prices from aggregated usage. B is about deploying in many Regions. D is about sizing capacity; the change here is how fast resources arrive and how cheap experiments become.
notes.explanation: Cutting the wait from weeks to minutes lowers the cost and time of experimenting, which is the agility the whitepaper describes.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: This results in a dramatic increase in agility for the organization, since the cost and time it takes to experiment and develop is significantly lower.

notes.front: A small charity’s only engineer spends most weeks replacing disks and fixing air-conditioning in its server room. The trustees want that time spent on services for beneficiaries. Which advantage applies?
notes.back: B: Stop spending money running and maintaining data centres
notes.choices:
A) Benefit from massive economies of scale
B) Stop spending money running and maintaining data centres
C) Go global in minutes
D) Trade fixed expense for variable expense
notes.choicesExplained: A is about the provider’s lower prices. C is about deploying in many Regions. D is about paying per use; the trustees’ aim is to stop doing the physical upkeep at all.
notes.explanation: The cloud lets you focus on your own customers rather than on racking, stacking and powering servers.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: Focus on projects that differentiate your business, not the infrastructure. Cloud computing lets you focus on your own customers, rather than on the heavy lifting of racking, stacking, and powering servers.

notes.front: A start-up notices that its cloud provider charges less per hour of computing than the start-up could achieve by running its own hardware. Which advantage explains the lower price?
notes.back: D: Benefit from massive economies of scale
notes.choices:
A) Stop guessing capacity
B) Increase speed and agility
C) Go global in minutes
D) Benefit from massive economies of scale
notes.choicesExplained: A is about sizing capacity. B is about how fast resources arrive. C is about deploying in many Regions; none of them explains a lower unit price.
notes.explanation: The provider aggregates usage from hundreds of thousands of customers, and the resulting scale translates into lower pay-as-you-go prices.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: Because usage from hundreds of thousands of customers is aggregated in the cloud, providers such as AWS can achieve higher economies of scale, which translates into lower pay as-you-go prices.

notes.front: A booking site runs all its instances in one Availability Zone. A power failure there takes the whole site offline for an afternoon. What change would best protect it next time?
notes.back: A: Run instances in more than one Availability Zone
notes.choices:
A) Run instances in more than one Availability Zone
B) Move to larger instances in the same zone
C) Buy the instances in advance at a discount
D) Re-use existing software licences
notes.choicesExplained: B keeps every instance in the one location that failed. C changes how you pay, not where instances run. D is about licensing, not availability.
notes.explanation: Launching instances in multiple Availability Zones protects applications from the failure of a single location.
notes.source: Amazon EC2 User Guide, “Regions and Zones”
notes.evidence: By launching EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones, you can protect your applications from the failure of a single location in the Region.

notes.front: A ticketing service adds servers automatically when a popular sale opens and removes them when demand falls. Which cloud benefit is this?
notes.back: C: Elasticity
notes.choices:
A) High availability
B) Bring Your Own License (BYOL)
C) Elasticity
D) Rightsizing
notes.choicesExplained: A is about surviving the failure of a location, not following demand. B is a licensing model. D is downsizing instances that are idle or under-used, not adding capacity for a peak.
notes.explanation: The exam guide links elasticity to auto scaling, which grows and shrinks capacity with the load.
notes.source: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) Exam Guide, “Content Domain 3: Cloud Technology and Services, Task Statement 3.3”
notes.evidence: Recognizing that auto scaling provides elasticity

notes.front: A manufacturer has several years left on database licences it bought for its own servers. It is moving those databases to the cloud and wants to keep using the licences. Which approach is this?
notes.back: B: Bring Your Own License (BYOL)
notes.choices:
A) Rightsizing
B) Bring Your Own License (BYOL)
C) Automation
D) Elasticity
notes.choicesExplained: A is downsizing under-used instances. C is replacing manual effort with automated processes. D is scaling capacity with demand; none of them is about licences.
notes.explanation: Bring Your Own License means re-purposing your existing licence inventory for your cloud resources, which can save costs.
notes.source: AWS License Manager User Guide, “What is AWS License Manager?”
notes.evidence: you can save costs by using Bring Your Own License model (BYOL) opportunities. That is, you can re-purpose your existing license inventory for use with your cloud resources.

notes.front: A report shows that a team’s large instances have run at very low utilisation for a month, although the team still needs them. What should it do to cut cost?
notes.back: A: Rightsize them to a smaller size
notes.choices:
A) Rightsize them to a smaller size
B) Move them to another Availability Zone
C) Re-use existing licences on them
D) Add more instances of the same size
notes.choicesExplained: B changes where they run, not how big they are. C changes licensing, not capacity. D adds even more unused capacity.
notes.explanation: The instances are still needed, so stopping them is out; downsizing low-utilisation instances reduces cost.
notes.source: How AWS Pricing Works (historical reference), “AWS Cost Optimization: Match capacity with demand”
notes.evidence: Use AWS Cost Explorer Resource Optimization to get a report of Amazon EC2 instances that are either idle or have low utilization. You can reduce costs by either stopping or downsizing these instances.

notes.front: Engineers rebuild each test environment by hand, and every copy turns out slightly different. Which benefit would address both the effort and the inconsistency?
notes.back: D: Automation
notes.choices:
A) Elasticity
B) Economies of scale
C) Rightsizing
D) Automation
notes.choicesExplained: A follows demand but does not build environments. B lowers the provider’s prices. C resizes existing instances; none of them replaces the manual rebuild.
notes.explanation: Automation creates and replicates workloads at low cost and avoids the expense of manual effort.
notes.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, “General design principles”
notes.evidence: Automation permits you to create and replicate your workloads at low cost and avoid the expense of manual effort.

notes.front: Which of these is one of the three fundamental drivers of cost in the pricing whitepaper?
notes.back: C: Outbound data transfer
notes.choices:
A) Inbound data transfer
B) Data transfer between services in the same Region
C) Outbound data transfer
D) The number of people using the console
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: in most cases neither is charged, although the whitepaper notes exceptions. D is not among the drivers, which are compute, storage and outbound data transfer.
notes.explanation: Outbound transfer is a driver; inbound and same-Region transfer are usually free, which is a common trap.
notes.source: How AWS Pricing Works (historical reference), “Key principles: Understand the fundamentals of pricing”
notes.evidence: There are three fundamental drivers of cost with AWS: compute, storage, and outbound data transfer.

notes.front: Which arrangement is cloud computing?
notes.back: B: Getting storage and databases over the internet on demand and paying as you go
notes.choices:
A) Buying servers for your own building and paying for them up front
B) Getting storage and databases over the internet on demand and paying as you go
C) Leasing a fixed rack in a shared building for five years
D) Buying software licences once and installing them on office computers
notes.choicesExplained: A is an upfront hardware investment. C commits to fixed capacity for years. D is a one-off software purchase; none of them is on-demand delivery with pay-as-you-go pricing.
notes.explanation: The definition has two parts, on-demand delivery over the internet and pay-as-you-go pricing, and only this option has both.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “What is cloud computing?”
notes.evidence: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute power, database, storage, applications, and other IT resources through a cloud services platform via the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.

notes.front: How does a fixed expense differ from a variable expense in the six advantages?
notes.back: Fixed: invest heavily in data centres and servers before you know the use. Variable: pay only when, and as much as, you consume.
notes.explanation: The difference is timing and certainty: a fixed expense commits money before use is known, a variable one follows use.
notes.source: Overview of Amazon Web Services, “Six advantages of cloud computing”
notes.evidence: Instead of having to invest heavily in data centers and servers before you know how you’re going to use them, you can pay only when you consume computing resources, and pay only for how much you consume.

notes.front: Which two licensing strategies does the exam guide ask you to tell apart?
notes.back: The Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model, and included licences.
notes.explanation: With BYOL you re-use licences you already hold; the guide sets it against licences that come included rather than brought.
notes.source: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) Exam Guide, “Content Domain 1: Cloud Concepts, Task Statement 1.4”
notes.evidence: Understanding the differences between licensing strategies (for example, Bring Your Own License [BYOL] model compared with included licenses)
